title: Case 1: Administration of Union Territories & Role of Administrator/LG (Article 239 • Writ Petition)
legalTheme: Part VIII: The Union Territories • Article 239
factualMatrix: Before the Supreme Court of India (Article 32), an aggrieved petitioner challenged an impugned executive notification and enforcement order issued by the Union Ministry / Central Authority under Article 239 (Administration of Union Territories & Role of Administrator/LG) of Part VIII (The Union Territories). Relying on the core guarantee that Provides for the direct administration of every Union Territory by the President, acting through an Administrator appointed by him with such designation as he specifies (such as Lieutenant Governor or Chief Commissioner). and citing Govt. of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India (2018), the petitioner sought judicial invalidation for violating constitutional limits and procedural fairness.
framingQuestions: 1. Whether the Writ Petition before the Supreme Court of India (Article 32) is maintainable under Article 239?
2. Does the Union Ministry / Central Authority's executive notification and enforcement order conform to Article 239 (Administration of Union Territories & Role of Administrator/LG)?
3. How does Govt. of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India (2018) govern the constitutional validity and relief in this matter?
statutoryApplicability: Govt. of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India (2018)
modelAnswer:
1. MAINTAINABILITY: The Writ Petition before the Supreme Court of India (Article 32) is maintainable as it raises a direct constitutional question under Article 239 (Part VIII).

2. SUBSTANTIVE ANALYSIS (Article 239): Provides for the direct administration of every Union Territory by the President, acting through an Administrator appointed by him with such designation as he specifies (such as Lieutenant Governor or Chief Commissioner). Applying the governing principle—'Administered by the President acting through an Administrator / Lieutenant Governor (Art 239).'—the impugned executive notification and enforcement order by the Union Ministry / Central Authority must strictly satisfy constitutional bounds.

3. PRECEDENT (Govt. of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India (2018)) & RELIEF: Guided by Govt. of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India (2018), any overreach inconsistent with Article 239 is liable to be quashed or suitably restrained.

markingRubric.criterion: Precedent reasoning (Govt. of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India (2018)) & relief

factualMatrix: Before the Supreme Court of India (Article 32), an aggrieved petitioner challenged an impugned licensing or regulatory restriction issued by the Union Ministry / Central Authority under Article 241 (High Courts for Union Territories (J&K, Ladakh & Delhi)) of Part VIII (The Union Territories). Relying on the core guarantee that Empowers Parliament by law to constitute a High Court for a Union Territory or declare any court in any such territory to be a High Court for all or any of the purposes of the Constitution. and citing Govt. of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India (2018), the petitioner sought judicial invalidation for violating constitutional limits and procedural fairness.
framingQuestions: 1. Whether the Writ Petition before the Supreme Court of India (Article 32) is maintainable under Article 241?
2. Does the Union Ministry / Central Authority's licensing or regulatory restriction conform to Article 241 (High Courts for Union Territories (J&K, Ladakh & Delhi))?
3. How does Govt. of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India (2018) govern the constitutional validity and relief in this matter?
statutoryApplicability: Govt. of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India (2018)
modelAnswer:
1. MAINTAINABILITY: The Writ Petition before the Supreme Court of India (Article 32) is maintainable as it raises a direct constitutional question under Article 241 (Part VIII).

2. SUBSTANTIVE ANALYSIS (Article 241): Empowers Parliament by law to constitute a High Court for a Union Territory or declare any court in any such territory to be a High Court for all or any of the purposes of the Constitution. Applying the governing principle—'Parliament retains plenary overriding legislative competence over Union Territories under Art 246(4).'—the impugned licensing or regulatory restriction by the Union Ministry / Central Authority must strictly satisfy constitutional bounds.

3. PRECEDENT (Govt. of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India (2018)) & RELIEF: Guided by Govt. of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India (2018), any overreach inconsistent with Article 241 is liable to be quashed or suitably restrained.

factualMatrix: Before the District & Sessions Court, an aggrieved petitioner challenged an impugned licensing or regulatory restriction issued by the Statutory Commission / Regulatory Board under Article 241 (High Courts for Union Territories (J&K, Ladakh & Delhi)) of Part VIII (The Union Territories). Relying on the core guarantee that Empowers Parliament by law to constitute a High Court for a Union Territory or declare any court in any such territory to be a High Court for all or any of the purposes of the Constitution. and citing Govt. of NCT of Delhi v.
